text:
Einstein didn't fail math. He excelled at it and had mastered calculus by about 15. The myth likely came from a misread of a Swiss grading scale (where 6 was the top mark) and from his leaving a German school early. He did fail the entrance exam to the Zurich Polytechnic at 16, but only because of the non-science sections; his math and physics scores were exceptional. If you tell your kid the myth, it can backfire when they look it up.

"Grades don't matter" is also not quite true, and kids tend to notice. Grades affect course placement, scholarships, and college options, so the claim can cost you credibility.

A more accurate message that still takes the pressure off: grades are feedback on how well something is being learned right now, not a measure of intelligence or worth. They matter as information and for some opportunities, but a bad grade is a problem to diagnose (misunderstood material? not enough practice? a bad test day?), not a verdict. Pair that with praise and attention for effort, curiosity, and recovery from setbacks, so your response to a bad grade is "what happened, and what do we try next?" rather than disappointment or dismissal.

If you want a real example of struggle and persistence, Thomas Edison's teachers reportedly called him slow (also partly embellished), so a better pick is someone with a documented setback, such as Michael Jordan being cut from his varsity team as a sophomore (though he was placed on JV, not totally cut from basketball) or J.K. Rowling's many publisher rejections.
